analysis.one_liner: Raises federal low-income housing tax credit allocations to states to build more affordable rentals.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have permanently increased each state's annual allocation of the federal low-income housing tax credit, never received a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would increase the annual per-capita allocation every state receives for the low-income housing tax credit, stepping it up from $1.75 to $2.35 per person in 2017 and reaching $3.53 per person by 2021, with a permanent increase taking effect after 2022. States use these tax credits to help finance construction of rental apartments affordable to low- and moderate-income families. The credits are awarded to developers, who sell them to corporate investors, so the subsidies flow through private financing.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income renters, who gain access to more apartments built with capped, below-market rents; state housing agencies, which get more resources to allocate; and the developers and corporate investors who finance the projects.

how_it_helps.text: Raises each state's per-capita allocation of the low-income housing tax credit from $1.75 to $2.35 in 2017, stepping up to $2.59 in 2018, $2.82 in 2019, $3.06 in 2020, $3.29 in 2021, and $3.53 thereafter, while raising the minimum ceiling for small states from $2,000,000 to $2,710,000 and up to $4,065,000 [S3].

The increases are permanent: after 2022 the per-capita amount and ceiling become fixed at $3.53 and $4,065,000, and cost-of-living adjustments are re-based from 2002 to 2017 so future inflation raises the allocation further [S3].

The low-income housing tax credit is the main federal program financing privately built rental housing with rents capped for low-income tenants; larger state allocations mean more such apartments get built [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally, since expanded tax credits reduce federal revenue, and the subsidy is partly absorbed by the developers, syndicators, and investors who intermediate the credits rather than passed through in full to housing.

drawbacks.text: Roughly a third or more of the credit's value can be absorbed by intermediaries and developers rather than reaching housing, making it an expensive way to deliver a subsidy compared with direct programs; this is a general feature of the credit the bill expands, not a provision of the bill itself.

New affordable units built with the credit tend to concentrate in higher-income neighborhoods rather than the lowest-income areas, and rising subsidies can pull private development into tax-credit projects at the expense of units that would otherwise be built without subsidy; these are ongoing debates about the credit's design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Expanding the credit is a proven way to add capped-rent apartments for low-income families, and the bill's increases are substantial. The tradeoff is cost and efficiency: the tax-credit mechanism is one of the pricier ways to produce affordable housing, with part of the federal subsidy captured by the financing chain rather than the tenant. The bill leaves those design questions untouched; it simply scales up the existing program.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-WA) introduced the bill on October 31, 2017, with Reps. Adam Smith (D-WA) and Pramila Jayapal (D-WA) as original cosponsors [S1,S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation [S1,S5].
No further action is recorded: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote, through the end of the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death means no new federal revenue was spent on expanded housing credits; developers, investors, and state agencies gain nothing beyond the existing program, while low-income renters gain no additional affordable units from this bill. The outcome mostly preserves the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo — no new housing subsidy, no new cost

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, but no vote ever occurred and no recorded opposition is in the record; the bill simply stalled in committee without a floor test.

industries.note: More state tax-credit allocation means more financed projects and development fees for this industry, and the same projects produce capped-rent apartments for low-income renters. Part of the subsidy, however, is absorbed by the financing chain rather than reaching tenants.

industries.industry: Corporate tax-credit investors (large banks and insurers)
industries.note: These investors buy the credits to reduce their federal tax bills; a larger allocation gives them more credit to purchase. Their gain comes from federal revenue that would otherwise fund other priorities, though it is tied to producing housing for low-income people.
Each state's annual allocation would roughly double over the phase-in, giving state agencies more resources to allocate to local affordable housing projects.
